claims.text: A liquid-phase precursor route can lower the formation temperature of single-phase ZrB2 from above 2300 °C to approximately 1800 °C.
Liquid-phase precursor processing of ZrB2 will produce nanoscale or ultrafine grains.
The lower-temperature precursor route will produce well-densified ZrB2 with fewer pores.
The precursor-processed ZrB2 will have improved structural integrity during prolonged liquid plating-bath exposure.
Conventional single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering above 2300 °C.
Conventionally sintered ZrB2 typically has larger grains than precursor-processed ZrB2.
Conventionally sintered ZrB2 typically has more residual porosity and lower mechanical strength.
A liquid-phase precursor method enables atomic-scale mixing.
Single-phase ZrB2 can be prepared at approximately 1800 °C under an inert or reducing atmosphere using the proposed route.
Precursor processing forms uniformly dispersed nanoscale particles.
Transient liquid phases generated during precursor processing facilitate rapid densification.
Liquid precursors alter the reaction pathway and lower the activation energy for ZrB2 phase formation.
Lower-temperature processing produces a more uniform ZrB2 microstructure with fewer defects.
A more uniform microstructure with fewer defects mitigates hole development and structural degradation in a liquid plating bath.
Precursor-processed ZrB2 will have greater densification and mechanical strength than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
Precursor-processed ZrB2 will develop fewer holes, show less weight change, and resist component failure better during plating-bath exposure.
Liquid-phase approaches have successfully produced ultrafine diboride ceramic powders at temperatures up to 1800 °C.
The degree of ZrB2 microstructural refinement and its long-term plating-bath stability remain quantitatively undetermined.
A controlled comparison will use conventionally sintered ZrB2 and precursor-processed ZrB2 specimens exposed to the same plating bath for 200 hours.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in porosity, strength, and bath-induced degradation will falsify the hypothesis.
